Tejas called at eight: "Can you help me shift flats tomorrow? The truck's at seven."

We did the tree-planting drive on Sunday! Two hundred saplings along the canal near our school. My hands are still full of blisters and I'm weirdly proud of them.
But I keep thinking about your last letter. The river in your town rising so fast, your neighbours' houses under water, the school closed for two weeks. I saw the news too. People I'll never meet, sitting on rooftops.
Our teacher explained how cutting forests upstream makes floods worse downstream. It made me feel angry and also kind of helpless. I planted my forty trees and thought: is this even anything?
But maybe it's how it starts. My trees here. Your river there. It's all one river, somehow.
Write back and tell me you're safe.
Manjula

In the village of Ranipur, the brick kilns brought families from far away every winter. Their children didn't go to school.
Pradeep, twenty-four, taught maths at the government school. Every evening at six, under the neem tree, he ran a free class. Local kids came, and now so did six children from the kiln families.
Some villagers grumbled. "Why teach outsiders?"
"They're children," Pradeep said. "That's enough."
Avni, a nurse at the clinic, started coming on Thursdays to teach hand-washing songs. The children sang them loudly.
Pradeep had once dreamed of fixing the whole education system. Now he fixed one long-division problem at a time.
On election day he stood in line early, having read every candidate's record at the panchayat office. Then he went back to the neem tree.

Shalini, you're begging your mother to let you try the giant swing at the fair. Let me tell you about me at nine.
I'm Vijay, your Dada, and I had to try everything new. The tallest slide at the mela. The first ride on a neighbour's cycle. Sitting still bored me more than a scraped knee ever hurt.
One summer I climbed the big tamarind tree higher than anyone. I slipped on the way down and scraped my whole leg.
My father didn't forbid me. He said, "Climb, but learn how." He showed me which branches held, how to keep three hands and feet on the tree. That made climbing more exciting, not less.
So try the swing. Hold the bar tight, and let your mother watch.

qa.q: What tree did young Vijay climb?
qa.a: The big tamarind tree.

qa.q: What was young Vijay feeling when sitting still?
qa.a: He felt bored and restless, finding stillness worse than a scraped knee.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Vijay's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: His father teaching him how to climb safely was the turning point, because it let him keep the thrill while learning to manage the risk.

qa.q: How might Vijay's father have felt seeing the scraped leg?
qa.a: He was probably worried but calm, choosing to teach rather than forbid.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, he craved new thrills and learned safer ways to enjoy them.

The water park closed at five, the queues were long, and Ganga had one hour left and a headache. But Yogesh, eight, was pulling her hand towards the tallest slide.
"That one, Amma! Please! I've done all the small ones five times!"
"It's very high, Yogesh."
"The small ones are boring. I want the big one!"
They queued for thirty minutes in the sun. At the top, the lifeguard measured Yogesh against the height board. He was tall enough, just.
Ganga watched from below, heart thumping. He came shooting out of the tunnel with a scream that turned into laughter, water everywhere.
"AGAIN!" he shouted, before he'd even stood up.
Ganga checked the clock: twenty minutes. "Once more. Then home."
He was already running.

qa.q: How long did they queue for the tallest slide?
qa.a: Thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he came out of the tunnel?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and joyful, bursting with excitement to go again.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that kept the thrill safe?
qa.a: She queued with him, let the lifeguard check his height and watched from below, allowing the new challenge within safe limits.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel watching from below?
qa.a: She felt nervous, with her heart thumping, while he enjoyed the excitement.

grounding: It shows a child begging to try the tallest slide because excitement feels like life and boredom feels worse.

A new trampoline park had opened at the Andheri mall, and Suraj, ten, had talked of nothing else for a week.
"Can we go? Please? I'll do my homework on the bus."
His sister Rajni, sixteen, sighed. "You've been to the park, the pool, the cricket nets, all this month."
"But those are old! This is new!"
She took him on Saturday. Inside, Suraj didn't go to the small trampolines. He went straight to the foam pit and the high wall.
The staff made everyone wear grip socks and listen to the safety rules, while Suraj bounced from foot to foot.
Then he jumped, flipped halfway, landed in the foam and came up shouting with joy.
"Rajni! It's the BEST!"
Going home, he asked about the climbing wall in Thane.

The class was going on a nature walk, but it had started drizzling, the teacher was late, and everyone was waiting in two neat lines in the corridor. Chandrika, ten, stood exactly where she'd been told, her shoes lined up with the tile.
In the new school she did everything right. Same plait as the other girls. Same way of saying "Achha, fine." Never out of line.
Imran, beside her, whispered, "This walk is stupid. We should do it in the library instead."
Chandrika actually agreed. She'd been thinking the same.
When the teacher arrived and asked, "Anyone want to suggest something else?" Chandrika opened her mouth, then closed it. Everyone else was quiet.
They went out in the rain. Her shoes got soaked. She said nothing all the way.

qa.a: The tile.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she opened and closed her mouth?
qa.a: She felt afraid of disapproval and held back her own opinion, though she agreed with Imran.

qa.q: What small step could help Chandrika share her opinions?
qa.a: She could start by telling a trusted friend like Imran or the teacher privately, so speaking up feels less risky.

qa.q: How might Imran see Chandrika's silence?
qa.a: Imran might think Chandrika didn't agree, not knowing she had the same idea but was afraid to say it.

grounding: It shows a child following every rule and group habit out of fear of disapproval, burying her own opinion.

passage:
Manoj, eleven, never broke a rule in his Pune school. He wore his tie exactly right, used the same slang as the boys in his group, laughed at the same jokes.
On Friday Tarun, the group's leader, said, "We're not going to Kunal's birthday. He's weird."
Everyone nodded. Manoj nodded too.
But inside, Manoj didn't agree. Kunal had helped him with maths all year. He'd wanted to go.
That evening Kunal messaged: "Coming tomorrow?" Manoj stared at the phone for a long time.
He typed "Yes!" and deleted it. Typed "Sorry, busy." Deleted it.
Finally he didn't reply at all. He sat on his bed, stomach tight, feeling like someone who wasn't quite himself.

qa.q: What did Kunal help Manoj with all year?
qa.a: Maths.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling as he typed and deleted replies?
qa.a: He felt torn and anxious, afraid of the group's disapproval but uneasy going against his own opinion.

qa.q: What could Manoj try next?
qa.a: He could quietly go to the birthday or at least reply kindly to Kunal, even if the group disagrees.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when Manoj doesn't reply?
qa.a: Kunal would probably feel hurt and confused, since Manoj was someone he'd helped all year.

grounding: It shows a child following his group's rules and opinions for fear of disapproval, burying his own view.
